en: Granularity is what makes both affordable. One capability per declaration, one module per subject, means a test names one behaviour and a reader looking for it opens one file. Most of that is already enforced and this rule does not restate it: the registry refuses a capability declared outside its own module's namespace, and refuses a duplicate identity — <t1/>, proved by case <n1/>. Repeating a check that already exists would be the second registry this repository spends its time removing. What the registry cannot see is a module composed into the application that declares no command at all, and that is the one granularity finding this rule adds.
cs: Granularita je to, co umožňuje obojí. Jedna schopnost na deklaraci, jeden modul na předmět znamená, že test pojmenovává jedno chování a čtenář, který ho hledá, otevře jeden soubor. Většina toho je už vynucena a toto pravidlo to neopakuje: registr odmítne schopnost deklarovanou mimo jmenný prostor jejího modulu a odmítne duplicitní identitu — <t1/>, dokázáno případem <n1/>. Opakovat kontrolu, která už existuje, by znamenalo druhý registr, jehož odstraňováním toto repozitář tráví čas. Co registr vidět nemůže, je modul složený do aplikace, který nedeklaruje žádný příkaz, a to je jediné zjištění granularity, které toto pravidlo přidává.

en: Where the merge would conflict, or would change only derived output, <t1/> is asked as well. When every commit the head has and master lacks is on master already as an equal patch, the relation is <t2/>: the change landed, by a cherry-pick say, and master moved past it. A partial match never gives it. Neither does a head with a merge commit of its own in that range, because a merge's resolution has no patch to compare, nor a clean merge that changes authored paths: there master lacks something the head carries, such as a landed change that master has reverted since.
